title: A Dog's Life
byline: Written, produced, and directed by Charlie Chaplin; distributed by First National Pictures (1918)

evidence.note: Published 14 April 1918. Under US law the maximum copyright term for a pre-1978 work is 95 years from publication date (28-year initial + renewal, as extended by the CTEA). That term ran out in 2013 (1918 + 95). As of 2026 the print is in the public domain regardless of whether a renewal was ever filed.
evidence.source: Cornell Copyright Term and the Public Domain in the United States â€” authoritative term chart

evidence.note: The 1918 film is a silent picture; no synchronized score existed in 1918. Charlie Chaplin composed a new orchestral score in 1959 for a theatrical re-release. That 1959 score is a separate, still-protected work. Timothy Brock restored the Chaplin score for live performance (world premiere Bologna, Cinema Ritrovato 2003) and created a reduced-orchestra version in 2004. Both the 1959 Chaplin score and Brock's 2003 arrangement carry independent copyright. Virtually every commercially-circulating version of the film uses one of these protected sound elements.
evidence.source: Timothy Brock â€” A Dog's Life score page (composer's own site confirming 1959 Chaplin authorship and 2003 Brock restoration)

evidence.note: The screenplay is an original story by Charlie Chaplin with no identified prior literary source; it was published as part of the 1918 film. The same 95-year maximum US term applies (1918 + 95 = 2013). The story copyright has expired.
evidence.source: Cornell Copyright Term and the Public Domain in the United States â€” authoritative term chart

evidence.note: 'CHARLIE CHAPLIN,' 'THE LITTLE TRAMP,' and related character images are active trademarks and service marks owned by Bubbles Incorporated S.A., a Chaplin estate company. Roy Export S.A.S. also holds marks. These rights survive copyright expiry and independently restrict commercial use of the Tramp character's likeness and Chaplin's name.

watch.label: A Dog's Life (1918) â€” Charlie Chaplin; Internet Archive

editorial:
"A Dog's Life" was the first film Charlie Chaplin completed under his landmark $1 million contract with First National Pictures, signed in 1917. Released April 14, 1918, the 33-minute comedy was shot at Chaplin's own studio on Lillian Way, Los Angeles, and photographed by Roland Totheroh. Chaplin plays the Tramp alongside Edna Purviance as a dance-hall singer; the stray dog Scraps was played by a real dog the production acquired. The 1918 print entered the public domain no later than 2013, when the 95-year maximum US copyright term from its publication year ran out, and unscored copies circulate freely on the Internet Archive.

The live rights trap here is twofold and easy to walk into. First, Chaplin composed a synchronized orchestral score in 1959 for a theatrical re-release, and conductor Timothy Brock restored that score in 2003; every widely-distributed version of the film carries one of these protected sound elements, both controlled by Roy Export S.A.S. A creator who lifts footage from a scored copy is not working from public-domain material. Second, the Tramp characterâ€”costume, gait, and likenessâ€”is an active trademark held by Bubbles Incorporated S.A., a Chaplin estate entity separate from the copyright holder. Copyright expiry did not extinguish those marks. A documentary quoting silent footage is on firm ground; an advertisement or branded product featuring the Tramp is not.
faq: Can I freely use footage from this film?

The 1918 silent print is in the public domain; you can use it. The catch is sound: nearly every copy in wide distribution uses Chaplin's 1959 score or Brock's 2003 restoration of it, both still under copyright and controlled by Roy Export S.A.S. Download a mute (silent) copy from the Internet Archive and add your own music or silence.
The film is public domain â€” does that mean the Tramp character is free to use commercially?

No. Copyright and trademark are separate bodies of law. Bubbles Incorporated S.A. holds active trademark and personality rights over the Little Tramp character and Chaplin's likeness. You can quote the film; you cannot use the Tramp as a brand mark, in advertising, or on merchandise without a license from the Chaplin estate.
